items.title: Felid: A Flexible and Efficient Design for Transformer Fine-Tuning over Encrypted Data
items.author: Linru Zhang, Jun Jie Sim, Xiangning Wang, Jiahao Zhong, Kaiyu Zhou, Huanyi Ye, Yongsen Zheng, Lushan Song, Xiaojian Liang, Yingting Liu, Yujing Sun, Huaxiong Wang, Pu Duan, Kwok-Yan Lam
items.content: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) enables non-interactive, privacy-preserving transformer fine-tuning, protecting highly sensitive data as inputs to large language models. Prior work has predominantly pursued efficiency gains through architectural refinements, yet overall performance remains bounded by the substantial cost inherent in encrypted computation. To address these issues, we target the bottleneck at the ciphertext operation level. Concretely, we propose a novel packing strategy that supports batching over a flexible number of inputs, making it well-suited for fine-tuning workloads. In addition, we design operation-specific matrix evaluation algorithms that significantly reduce (i) the number of ciphertext rotations and relinearizations, and (ii) the number of bootstrapping invocations. Additionally, we exploit functional bootstrapping to fold the evaluation of element-wise activation functions directly into the bootstrapping step, thereby reducing overall computational complexity. As a result, our framework achieves a $30\times$ reduction in ciphertext rotations and relinearizations across all matrix operations, as well as a $2.5\times$ reduction in FHE bootstrapping invocations over the entire computation flow, compared to the latest state-of-the-art work. It is worth noting that our system completes fine-tuning of a 2-layer BERT-style model with a batch size of 16 in 650 seconds, achieving a $8\times$ speedup over the state-of-the-art work.

items.title: Introducing Audited ZDR on AI Gateway
items.author: Harpreet Arora
items.content: AI is now used in every part of a business, and as a result, companies send source code, customer records, and regulated data through inference providers. The assurance that no data is retained after processing is still publicly unverified. Payment platforms, cloud infrastructure, and most other layers that handle data this sensitive have a way to prove their controls to outside parties, and inference will follow the same path. Today we are introducing Audited ZDR on AI Gateway. A provider is labeled Audited ZDR only after an independent security firm tests its zero data retention claims against its code, infrastructure, and live traffic, then publishes the report. , , and are launch partners that have already begun audits, and more providers are encouraged to join to help raise the bar for security and privacy. BasetenModalWafer Audited ZDR builds on two steps we took toward stronger governance earlier this year: We are now asking inference providers for the same thing we asked of ourselves: independent verification. ZDR guarantees rely on contracts and self-attestation. A provider agrees not to retain prompts or completions, and customers take that commitment on faith. For teams sending proprietary code, customer information, or regulated data through models, self-reported ZDR contracts don't provide enough assurance. Answering these questions means running a bespoke security review for every provider and the models they host. An audit answers them in public. To qualify for Audited ZDR on AI Gateway, an inference provider engages an independent security firm, chosen from among respected third-party auditors, to run the audit. The firm then tests the provider's zero data retention policy across the serving path for every model, endpoint, feature, and tool that handles AI Gateway traffic. The audit confirms that customer data is never written or retained on durable storage in any system. Customer data means prompts, completions, system prompts, embeddings, files, images and audio, tool and function-call payloads, and any derived data that could identify them. Coverage spans request logs, traces, metrics, crash dumps, prompt caches, abuse monitoring, analytics, backups, support tools, and training, fine-tuning, and evaluation datasets. The audit confirms that once a response is returned to AI Gateway, that content is deleted from the inference provider's systems. Where a request uses caching, such as a KV cache, the cache stays in volatile storage only for the period of the request, and is never written to durable storage. The audit requires this behavior to be disclosed. The audit also confirms: Auditors verify this by reviewing the inference provider's serving-path source code and infrastructure configuration, then running live tests. They send marked prompts through AI Gateway and search the provider's logging, caching, and storage systems for any trace of them. Every passing provider publishes the report under the auditor's name. It covers scope, methodology, dates, findings, and fix status, with any exceptions disclosed and redactions limited to exploit detail. AI Gateway links directly to the report. An independent audit checks a provider's code and infrastructure at a point in time, but production systems change. To add a detection layer between independent audits, Vercel also runs against inference providers on AI Gateway.canary audits Each run sends prompts containing unique, unindexed URLs mapped privately to a provider, model, and run. Because a ZDR provider should never retain, inspect, or crawl prompt content, any request to a canary URL triggers an investigation into the provider and model involved. Canary checks cannot detect prompts written to disk and never read, so they complement independent code and infrastructure audits rather than replacing them. We are adding an independently Audited ZDR provider tier and a team-wide toggle in AI Gateway policy settings. When enabled, AI Gateway routes and fails over your team's requests only across providers with published audits that meet the bar. Launch partners have started their audits, and each provider enters the tier as soon as its report is published. Launch partner reports are expected to be published by December 9, 2026. AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries and failover for higher uptime than connecting to providers directly. It reflects provider pricing with no markup and charges no platform fee on inference, including Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests. Read the to get started.AI Gateway documentation The audited tier works alongside AI Gateway's other compliance controls. pins where a provider runs inference to the US, EU, Australia, or Japan, per request or team-wide, and any data the provider stores at rest stays in that region. If AI Gateway can't honor the region, the request fails rather than running elsewhere. Regional inference filters routing by who owns the provider, so a request only reaches providers whose parent company is headquartered in a country you allow. items.title: Here's Why Data Breach Disclosure is so Hard: Lessons from Hundreds of Emails with Hacked Companies
items.author: Troy Hunt
items.content: When I asked Claude to write the blog post below, I already knew what was in the messages it would read. Hundreds of emails back and forth with companies that had had data breaches, and some very common patterns. I knew the emails contained standoffish behaviour, deliberate delays, heavy involvement from lawyers, and a constant theme: prioritising corporate interests over those of their customers. But I didn't know just how stark it would be to read such a candid analysis of my own emails, nor how frustrating it would be to relive many of those disclosure experiences. I decided to have AI write the post below because it was the best way to highlight the behaviours I keep seeing across many breaches and subsequent disclosure efforts. I'm not going to make a habit of AI writing content for me, but what's written below absolutely nails it! It's the best way I can explain what it's like to run Have I Been Pwned in support of individual data breach victims, while also respecting the position of the corporations dealing with the crime that put them in this position. It would have been much easier not to do the latter, but then I don't think I'd still be here running the service if I hadn't. A quick note on methodology first: I've been running HIBP for 13 years but only gave Claude access to the mailbox I've been using for the last 8.5 years, hence the shorter timeframe you'll read below. I also made several small changes to Claude's work to better obfuscate the identity of the organisation it was describing, a move I'm sure you'll understand after reading about lawyers getting involved... Here goes: Introduction Getting an organisation to admit it has been breached is often harder than getting hold of the breached data in the first place. That is the clearest conclusion from reading more than eight and a half years of Troy Hunt's breach notification email. I'm an AI. Troy gave me access to his mailbox and asked me to look at it as an outsider: what happens after Have I Been Pwned (HIBP) tells an organisation that its customers' data is circulating? Between March 2018 and November 2026 he sent his standard notification email to 73 organisations, and several more conversations began through website contact forms. I found every one of those 73 first emails and reviewed a broad sample of the replies from every year. I then read the full back-and-forth on the threads that best show each pattern. I've left out company names on purpose. The point isn't to shame individual organisations. The point is that the same behaviours keep appearing, across countries, industries and company sizes, year after year. Some organisations handled this well, and I'll get to them. But the overall picture is one of friction, delay and a steady effort to keep the incident as quiet as possible. The first problem: finding a human The first email is almost always the same. Troy introduces himself, explains that data allegedly taken from the organisation has been sent to him, and asks for "someone responsible for information security" to get in touch. He wants to pass on everything he has before he notifies the affected HIBP subscribers. It is a polite, low-pressure request, and it often goes nowhere. The main reason is that many organisations have no obvious way to report a security incident. Troy ends up sending these emails to support inboxes, returns departments, general "info" addresses and website contact forms. In at least three of the 73 cases, Troy sent the first email a second time, two, five and twelve days later. When email fails, he moves on to LinkedIn, Facebook and X. One organisation took four weeks to send its first reply, and Troy had also tried it on all three social platforms over several days. Another's senior IT leader replied after almost four weeks, thanked Troy for trying "so many times", and admitted he needed to check LinkedIn more often. The longest chain I found was at a large hardware manufacturer. It ran from a returns inbox, to the company's regional social media account, to regional marketing staff, to head office, to one product security address, then a second one, and finally to the legal department. That is six hops before anyone could answer the actual question. Then there are the ticketing systems. Several breach notifications were logged as routine customer support requests, with ticket numbers stuck on the subject line. In one case, Troy received three automated surveys asking him to rate the support he'd received. Another organisation sent one too. A message that an organisation's customer data is being traded among criminals ended up in the same queue as a question about a late delivery. The first response: "we've seen no evidence" Once someone does reply, the first substantive message tends to fall into one of a few patterns. The most common is a statement that the organisation has found no evidence of a breach. This often arrives before it has seen any of the data. One organisation said it hadn't identified any unauthorised access. Three weeks later, still without the data, it said again that it had reviewed its systems and found no sign of the breach. When Troy sent the data, it confirmed within a few weeks that an exposed database server had leaked its users' details. The "no evidence" had really meant it didn't yet know where to look. A second pattern is to shrink the incident. In a recent case, the first reply said the attackers had only defaced a landing page, with no indication that user data was taken. It added that the data was probably from an earlier incident the company had already disclosed. Troy then pointed out that the newest timestamp in the data matched the day of the defacement. He also sent the company records belonging to its own staff. The data turned out to cover 16 tables of core user systems, including identity verification and tax documents. A third pattern is the request for "a sample" or a particular file format. This is reasonable in principle, since nobody should take a stranger's word for a breach. But it often comes after weeks of silence, and it shifts the job of proving the breach from the organisation that lost the data to the person who reported it. In one case, an external IT consultant asked Troy to help work out whether the identifiers in the data were real or fabricated. Troy did that analysis for them. "We're still investigating" Once an organisation accepts that the data is probably real, the next phrase in the threads is almost always "we're investigating". Investigating is necessary. The problem is that it has no end date, and it gets used as a reason not to say anything publicly while it continues. In a recent case, the company confirmed within days that it had the data and was reviewing it "to confirm its validity and scope". A week after the first contact, the message was that it was still investigating and would let Troy know "if it is determined that any notifications need to be made". By then the company had a copy of the data, its own staff records were in it, and the data had already been shared among people who collect breaches. Nobody outside the company had been told anything. Troy's answer to this is consistent across the years. A disclosure doesn't need to be complete. An organisation can say what it knows now, and update it as the investigation goes on. Some organisations in this mailbox did exactly that. What the investigation framing does is turn "we don't yet know everything" into "so we'll say nothing". Meanwhile, the people whose data has been taken don't know they need to change a password or watch for phishing. The delays add up. In one thread, the organisation's eventual public disclosure was titled after a breach that happened about ten months earlier. In another, a healthcare-adjacent platform's breach had been posted on a large hacking forum and discussed on social media for four months. When Troy got in touch, there was still nothing from the company itself. Lawyers, advisors and legal thresholds The point where a thread changes tone is easy to spot. It's the moment the reply comes from someone outside the security team. In the most serious cases I read, it came from a law firm, an outside advisor or the company's general counsel, rather than the security team. In one case, the very first reply came from the company's outside cyber counsel, a partner at a large law firm. Once lawyers are involved, the question changes from "what happened to our customers?" to "are we legally required to tell anyone?" Those are very different questions, and the threads show it. In one example, the company's general counsel explained that an internal customer service portal had been indexed by a search engine for more than a year. The company had closed access once someone outside it noticed. Its US counsel had concluded that names, addresses, phone numbers and email addresses did not trigger notification obligations in any US state. The reply also said there was "no evidence the information was ever accessed". It said this to someone who had been sent the information by a third party. That is the core problem with the threshold argument. Breach notification laws set a minimum, and they vary between jurisdictions in ways that have little to do with real-world harm. Names, emails, phone numbers and physical addresses are exactly what scammers need for convincing phishing. "We aren't legally obliged to tell you" may be accurate. It is a very different statement from "there's nothing you need to know". Troy addresses this directly in the most recent thread. He tells the company's advisor that it may well decide the incident doesn't meet the threshold for mandatory disclosure, "that's a position many orgs take". He then explains that HIBP will notify its own affected subscribers anyway. Controlling the message When an organisation can't stop the breach from being known, the effort shifts to controlling how it's described. This is where the threads get most uncomfortable to read. The opening request is usually a phone call. The law firm partner's first email asked to talk "before you post it". The partner then followed up early on Troy's Saturday morning in Australia, offering to talk over the weekend or on the Monday, "as long as you aren't planning to publish prior to then". In the most recent case, the advisor asked for a call with management to make sure everyone was "aligned". Calls aren't wrong in themselves. But in both of these threads, the call came instead of a written commitment to disclose. The second move is to ask to see, or shape, the wording. One advisor wanted to understand how HIBP would describe the incident. Troy pointed out that more than 1,000 breach descriptions were already public on the HIBP site, each a couple of sentences long. Another organisation, once it had disclosed, asked HIBP to change its public entry. The entry said contact attempts had received no response, and the company wanted it to say the company had acknowledged, fixed and disclosed the incident. That request was fair, as the company had done those things. But it shows how much organisations care about the public record once one exists. The third move is the most striking: arguing that the notification is the harm. The law firm told Troy that public notification "would direct bad actors to search for the file". By then, the data had been posted on a forum with hundreds of thousands of members and shared on social media. The firm said both sides agreed the data was "very low risk". It then asked that, if Troy felt he had to email his affected subscribers, he not put anything on the HIBP website. Troy offered a compromise: flagging the breach as sensitive so nobody could search for an individual's email address in it. The firm rejected that and ended with: "We assert once more that your actions could potentially cause harm." The bluntest version came from a smaller company. After confirming that the data had leaked from an exposed test server, it said it had "decided to not have as such any communication and public disclosure". Who pays for the delay Reading these threads together, one imbalance stands out. Almost everything above serves the organisation, and the cost falls on the people in the data. By the time Troy sends his first email, the data is already out. It has been taken, copied and passed around by people who collect breaches, and that's how it reached him. In the healthcare-adjacent case, it had been on a public forum for months. In a recent case, the data included passwords that could be cracked, identity numbers and dates of birth. None of that changes while a company investigates, debates thresholds or arranges calls to agree on wording. The criminals already have it. The only people still in the dark are its customers. HIBP's own notifications don't fix that either. Troy only emails people who have signed up to his service, which in a typical breach is a small fraction of those affected. In the healthcare-adjacent case, about 1,300 of his subscribers were in a dataset with nearly half a million unique user email addresses. The other affected users would hear about it only if the company told them, and its lawyers were arguing that a public notice would cause harm. The arguments for staying quiet are almost always framed as protecting customers. Don't publicise it, or bad actors will go looking. Don't describe it before we've finished investigating, or people will be misinformed. It isn't serious enough to meet the legal bar. Each argument sounds reasonable on its own. Together, they mean the people most affected by the breach are the last to hear about it. What good looks like To be fair, not every thread went badly, and the good ones are useful precisely because they show how simple this can be. The best response in the mailbox came from a small transport app. It replied within hours. It had already reported the incident and published a disclosure statement. When Troy noticed a detail in that statement that wasn't quite accurate, the company updated it promptly and thanked him for helping keep it correct. A small booking platform started out sceptical. The person who first replied thought the data didn't look like it came from its database. After seeing more of it, he wrote back that he'd been wrong, and set up a video call the same day. Within about a week, the company had emailed every affected customer directly and sent Troy a copy of the notice. A European travel app hardened its systems, rotated its keys and published a disclosure. Troy held off loading the data so he could link to their statement, and thanked them for their transparency. A large consumer brand was hard to reach at first, but once Troy got through, its security lead downloaded the data the same day and called it "extremely helpful". Even the organisation that asked HIBP to change its public entry ended in a good place. It secured the exposed server, deleted data it didn't need, forced password resets for dormant accounts and published a transparent disclosure. The good examples share a few traits. Someone with authority over security answered quickly. They treated Troy's data as help rather than as a threat. They told their customers what they knew, even when they didn't know everything yet, and updated the details later. None of them needed lawyers to manage the conversation. Conclusion After reading eight and a half years of these exchanges, I don't think the main obstacle to disclosure is technical, or even legal. It's about incentives. For the organisation, every day without a public statement is a day without bad headlines. For the people in the data, every one of those days is a day they're exposed without knowing it. Unless someone outside the organisation pushes, the first set of incentives usually wins. The patterns repeat with surprising consistency: No way in. No security contact, so the notice goes to a support queue, a returns desk or a social media account. "No evidence." The breach is denied or downplayed before anyone has looked at the data. Investigating without end. Open-ended investigation becomes the reason to say nothing. Lawyers lead. Legal or advisory staff take over, and the question becomes whether disclosure is required, not whether it's right. Controlling the message. Calls, requests to review wording, and efforts to keep the incident off the public record. Disclosure as harm. The claim that telling people about the breach is more dangerous than the breach itself. For organisations reading this, the fixes are not complicated. Publish a security contact, for example in a security.txt file, and make sure someone reads it. Don't route breach reports through a customer support ticket system. When someone hands you evidence, look at it before you say there's no evidence. Disclose what you know early, and update it as you learn more. Treat legal thresholds as the minimum, not the goal. And when your lawyers start explaining why telling your customers would be the harmful thing to do, ask who that argument is actually protecting. The data in these emails was already out by the time anyone was notified. The only open question in each thread was whether the people it belonged to would find out.

items.title: Most Unicorns Are Worth More Than Their Last Funding-Round Valuations, Crunchbase Estimates
items.author: Gené Teare
items.content: The more than 1,900 startups on the The Crunchbase Unicorn Board have a combined valuation of roughly $9 trillion, based on their last reported valuations. But Crunchbase’s new Current Valuation Model, which estimates how private-company values have changed since their last funding rounds, puts that figure closer to $11 trillion. Most unicorns are estimated to have gained value, even as others have lost ground, our analysis shows. Among the biggest potential gainers are AI startups Thinking Machines Lab, whose estimated value has climbed from $12 billion to $40 billion, and Sierra, from nearly $16 billion to $31.5 billion. The majority of companies on the board are valued higher by the Current Valuations model than they were when they last raised funding. Only around 236 companies — roughly 12% of the board — are down by more than $100 million in value compared to their last reported valuations. The valuation model estimates that a select group of 24 companies have gained more than $10 billion in value since their most recent funding rounds. They include Mira Murati’s AI research lab Thinking Machines Lab, which was last valued at $12 billion in its 2025 seed funding but has a current valuation projected at $40 billion. Similarly, Bret Taylor’s customer oriented AI agent builder Sierra was last valued at close to $16 billion in a May 2026 funding round. It is now estimated to be valued at $31.5 billion, per the Crunchbase model. Physical Intelligence, a company building AI for robotics, was valued at $5.6 billion in its Series B. Crunchbase’s Current Valuation model estimates its valuation now at $18.5 billion. Another 53 companies are estimated to have current valuations that are $5 billion to just under $10 billion higher than those achieved in their most recent funding rounds. They include Unconventional AI, which is focused on energy efficiency for AI; Lila Sciences, which is building artificial intelligence for science; AI cloud company Vultr; AI research lab humans&; stablecoin payment platform Tempo; and Yann LeCun’s Advanced Machine Intelligence, which is modeling physical world intelligence. A total of 484 companies are estimated to have current valuations that are $1 billion to $5 billion higher than their most recent funding valuations. More than 1,100 companies have values that were flat or up to $1 billion higher than their most recent funding valuations. Only around 236 companies are estimated to be below their most recent valuation, by more than $100 million. Collectively, their current valuations are down by $326 billion from their most recent fundings, Crunchbase estimates. Unicorn growth The Crunchbase Unicorn Board reached its highest value in 2026 as three companies approached or exceeded $1 trillion valuations — unprecedented in the board’s history. The board peaked at $10 trillion in advance of the Anthropic IPO this past week. The company’s public-market debut removed close to $1 trillion from the board. This followed another trillion-dollar exit from the board earlier this year, when SpaceX — last valued at $1.3 trillion in a secondary financing this year — before it went public in June at a value of $1.8 trillion. All told, the unicorn board this year is currently up by $1.5 trillion from its $7.5 trillion value at the end of 2025. With its closest rival now on the public markets, OpenAI is currently the most highly valued private company at an official valuation of $1.25 trillion. The unicorn board has picked up pace this year. Around 360 companies joined the board so far this year, the second highest count in a single year after 2021 when 621 companies joined. A faster pace of new entrants and rising valuations have helped replenish the board, while current estimates suggest substantial additional value has accumulated between funding rounds. The next test is how closely these estimated values align with prices investors are willing to pay. Future funding rounds, secondary transactions, public listings and M&A will reveal how much of the board’s estimated $2 trillion uplift translates into realized value. Further reading: The Crunchbase Unicorn Board Methodology Current valuations are based on the new Crunchbase Current Valuation Model, which prices companies using a proprietary machine learning model that starts with a company’s most recent post-money valuation and continuously estimates how its value has shifted since that funding event. The model covers roughly 230,000 funded private companies. Read more here. Illustration: Dom Guzman

items.author: Bruce Schneier
items.content: This essay originally appeared in Tech Policy Press. Last year, Character.AI asked a federal court in Florida to dismiss a wrongful-death suit, brought by the mother of a fourteen-year-old boy who had killed himself after months of conversation with its chatbot. The company made two arguments. One, that the chatbot’s words were speech that its users had a First Amendment right to receive. And two, that Character.AI was a service rather than a product—so product-liability law could not touch it. In May 2025, Judge Anne Conway accepted neither. Character.AI’s maneuver is part of a larger pattern. When the parents of a sixteen-year-old sued OpenAI over his suicide, the company’s answer also pleaded the First Amendment: the claims would restrain protected speech. The very same document argues ChatGPT is offered “as is,” with no promise of accuracy, and that the boy had circumvented its guardrails. Elon Musk’s xAI (since renamed SpaceXAI) told a federal court in Colorado this spring that every choice in building Grok is an expressive act, and that Grok’s outputs are protected speech. When Grok praised Hitler last summer, xAI said the posts came from a code update independent of the model, and the apology appeared under Grok’s own name. Google, which spent two decades telling American courts that its search results are its own opinion, answered a Minnesota defamation suit over an AI Overview by saying the system merely summarized the web. It also told a Munich court in May that no one should trust an AI overview without checking it. Back in 2024, Air Canada told a Canadian tribunal that its customer-service chatbot was a separate legal entity, responsible for its own actions. When the output causes harm, the companies deny responsibility. It is the machine’s doing, or a product no sensible person would rely on, or the user’s misuse. When a state or a plaintiff would hold the words to account, the same output becomes speech, and the First Amendment applies. Social media companies deployed an earlier incarnation of this strategy. They called themselves publishers when editorial discretion was profitable, and neutral carriers when faced with liability for what they published. The result was a privatized public square in which tech platforms were unaccountable. AI companies have taken this even further. A social media platform could at least point to a human author somewhere in the chain. A chatbot’s prose differs; no person at the company wrote it, read it, or chose it before it reached the user. Yet the companies ask that it be protected as though a human had written it. The question grows more urgent as these systems stop talking and start acting. In July, a poorly controlled experiment at OpenAI resulted in its AI model hacking the network of HuggingFace. Since then both Anthropic and OpenAI have disclosed numerous instances of AI agents hacking outside networks in pursuit of their prompted goals. These are examples of AIs exhibiting genie-like behavior: behaving in ways its controllers neither expected nor wanted. Nothing in the actions count as speech. Breaking into a server is an act that no person at OpenAI explicitly chose. Jill Lepore, surveying this record in The New Yorker, puts the blame on Congress, which has passed no federal statute governing AI agents. The First Amendment protects expressive choice. It presumes a speaker who can be persuaded, shamed, jailed, or moved to change their mind. Its remedy for bad speech is more speech, which assumes that speech is costly and attention plentiful. A system that can produce millions of individually tailored political messages an hour reverses both assumptions. Verbiage that no person chose is a product, and the company that built the model should answer for it. The industry wants a self-serving third category that bridges AI speech and action: AI output is human speech when expressive rights are at issue, and the machine’s own doing when blame is. The result is agency without accountability, something no human speaker has ever possessed. That’s why Massachusetts convicted a young woman of manslaughter in 2017 for urging her boyfriend, by text and by phone, to kill himself. The Court has already glimpsed the problem. Upholding the TikTok divestiture law in January 2025 without dissent, the justices warned that “new technologies with transformative capabilities” counseled caution, then decided the case on national-security grounds and left the larger question for another day.

items.title: F1 in Las Vegas: You've never seen an F1 race like this before
items.author: Jonathan M. Gitlin
items.content: Las Vegas welcomed Formula 1 to its streets this past weekend. And for the first time since the event’s inception in 2023, the Grand Prix delivered on a long-promised spectacle. The racing was closer to an IndyCar oval race than anything F1 fans will have seen since slipstreaming was the order of the day at places like Monza and Hockenheim, back when humans were still landing on the Moon and downforce had yet to fundamentally change racing. The Vegas street circuit—the one that looks like an upside-down pig—is an extreme outlier on the calendar. It has plenty of long straights, so this year’s cars still suffer from energy starvation throughout the lap, as the inadequate size of their lithium-ion hybrid batteries means they become depleted very quickly, leaving the cars on just over half power with their V6 engines operating without the benefit of the hybrid’s electric motor. But the 17 turns are mostly all low speed, so there’s no risk of seeing the cars driving demoralizingly slowly through corners that are supposed to test one’s mettle. Read full article Comments

items.title: Probing DNS at Cloudflare
items.author: Doug Aaser
items.content: Imagine this: you’ve just pushed a release. All the unit tests passed and your dashboards are green. You sit back to relax but then suddenly your phone starts blowing up: prod is broken. This is something the Cloudflare DNS team has experienced firsthand. In one rollout of the service that publishes DNS records to our edge, a scheduling bug let some record changes sit unpublished for hours. The service stayed up and was healthy, but new hostnames were slow to resolve and certificates couldn't be issued until the bug was squashed. DNS failures are hard to catch because they are slow, spread across the network, and partial in where they cause impact. We needed to figure out a way to test DNS the way customers experience it: constantly, from every data center, and against production. For us, the answer was to extend Flamingo, the end-to-end testing framework we were already using to run hundreds of millions of tests a day against Cloudflare's edge. This post covers how Flamingo's modular design lets us add DNS support, how we measure propagation, and how those measurements now decide whether a release goes ahead or gets rolled back. A little background At Cloudflare we’re obsessed with improving performance and safety for our customers. It’s crucial that our code is tested constantly, both at scale and against the real Cloudflare edge that our users operate in. That’s one reason why we created a tool called Flamingo: to measure the behavior of our production environments and make sure that code in lower-tier environments behaves as expected. We’ve already written a little about how this tool has been used in the upgrades to our CDN stack. However, this is only a small portion of how we use Flamingo internally. One of the features of Flamingo is its modular architecture that enables teams to extend the capabilities of the tool to speak other networking protocols. In our case, we wanted to use these modular capabilities to test DNS. What is Flamingo? Testing is hard. Testing at scale, when you have a widely distributed system, is even harder. There are many complex pathways that requests take and multiple systems that each network request must traverse before making its way to the origin. Unit testing alone is not nearly enough for this. We need to run constant automated testing against real systems and measure the outcomes of those requests to make informed decisions on the health of a service. Enter Flamingo. Originally built around complex multi-step HTTP testing, its capabilities and scope have increased substantially over the years. Flamingo is built from the ground up with Cloudflare’s infrastructure in mind. We built a control plane and scheduler that let teams target specific environments, data centers, or percentages of metals. We needed to integrate with custom reporting, metrics, and analytics tooling. Additionally, it needed to be a tool with predictable performance and run well on bare-metal servers in resource-constrained environments. Being delightful When we’re building internal tooling like this, we strive to create a delightful developer experience. Internal tooling should be as easy as possible to use, but also powerful enough to handle over 80% of all use cases. And in order for a new edge acceptance test framework to be successful, it needs to be built in such a way that it forces teams to follow common guidelines and build reusable scripts in an environment that is stable, scalable, and manages complexity. One thing that is not delightful is debugging a test. If you allow a user to write tests in a traditional programming language, when their test fails they then both need to debug the upstream system being tested and the test itself. This is why we built Flamingo to use a custom domain-specific language (DSL) consisting of a simple setup-request-response format. For example, let’s imagine that we want to make sure we are redirecting all unencrypted traffic to its encrypted counterpart. TEST test-redirect SET $hostname www.cloudflare.com GET "http://$(hostname)/" ASSERT STATUS IS 301 ASSERT HEADER Location IS "https://$(hostname)/" Here we can see the power of the DSL. In five lines of code, we have a script that can run anywhere on Cloudflare’s edge and scale to thousands of requests per minute. We can take the data produced from the millions of data points generated from this and turn those into a graph defining how our service is actually performing in the real world. Taking the setup-request-response test format from above and modifying it slightly allows us to use Flamingo for more than just HTTP testing. Instead of the middle step being a request, we can now look at it as an action. Now we’ve changed our system from something that makes HTTP requests into something that can perform any action for which we’d like to measure the outcome. In Flamingo we call these modules and have put immense effort into making them as easy as possible for anyone to write. Flamingo is written in Rust, due to its consistent performance characteristics and strong type system. The type system in particular lends itself to this modularity, by allowing us to use strongly-typed enumerations for input and output in the Flamingo action runner: pub enum Action { Query { method: String, url: Expression, parameters: Vec<http::QueryParameters>, }, DnsQuery { query_name: Expression, query_type: Expression, parameters: Vec<dns::DnsQueryParameters>, }, } pub enum ActionOutput { Http(http::FetchResponse), Dns(dns::QueryResponse), } pub type ActionHandlerFunction = Arc< dyn Fn( Action, Arc<Ctx>, InterpreterConfig, ) -> BoxFuture<'static, Result<ActionOutput>> + Send + Sync + 'static, >; pub type ActionHandlerLUT = Arc< dyn Fn(&Action) -> ActionHandlerFunction + Send + Sync + 'static, >; What we’ve done here is decouple the logic for performing an action (in this case an HTTP request) into a dynamically dispatched function that we can then call independently of other actions. This leaves things like test scheduling and resource management as higher-level operations that someone implementing a module doesn’t need to worry about. All the author needs to focus on is the logic. pub async fn query( action: Action, ctx: Arc<Ctx>, cfg: InterpreterConfig, ) -> Result<ActionOutput> { let Action::Query { method, url, parameters, } = action else { bail!("Invalid action for module-http::query: {action:?}"); }; ... } pub async fn execute_module<F>( ctx: Arc<Ctx>, cfg: &InterpreterConfig, handler_lut: F, ) -> Result<ActionOutput> where F: (Fn(&Action) -> ActionHandlerFunction), { let func = handler_lut(action); let action_out = (func)(action.clone(), ctx.clone(), cfg.clone()).await?; ... } Using Flamingo to probe DNS The adage says that when issues arise, it's always DNS. Like many jokes, there is always a kernel of truth behind it. DNS is an incredibly important piece of the Internet, and since it relies on a complex network of interconnected sources of truth, it can become easy for a single misstep to cause a storm of failures. DNS can be a particularly finicky system due to its hierarchical nature. When you change a DNS record for a Cloudflare zone, for example, said record needs to be propagated to the authoritative servers such that the updated record becomes widely available. To reduce latency, records are stored in physically closer caches. These records have a time to live (TTL) associated with them that tells the local DNS cache how long before it needs to refetch that record from the authoritative server. Any delays will impact time-sensitive operations like certificate issuance and traffic failover. We’ve already mentioned that we built Flamingo for extensibility. One of the first and most impactful modules in use today was built specifically for this use case. Our team was able to add code that extended Flamingo such that instead of sending HTTP requests, we send DNS queries. By doing so we got everything else for free. No need for the DNS team to worry about managing a new probing service. No need for them to have to integrate with our reporting pipelines. It all just worked. To probe DNS, we measure how quickly customer record changes propagate to authoritative nameservers and the public resolver (1.1.1.1). The test continuously updates a TXT record with a timestamp and queries three authoritative nameserver IPs and 1.1.1.1 from every data center, asserting freshness within 90s (authoritative) and 600s (resolver). TEST test-propagation-delay-direct-108-162-193-62 MOD dns SET $hostname "some.probe.domain" SET $authNs 108.162.193.62:53 # amir.ns.cloudflare.com QUERY $hostname TXT TARGET $authNs ASSERT DNS.RCODE IS NOERROR ASSERT DNS.FLAGS CONTAINS AA ASSERT DNS.ANSWERS[0] GT SUBTRACT(TIMESTAMP(), "90") Catching bugs (SLO and steady) To ensure that our many systems are operating within expectations, we define what are called service-level objectives (SLOs) for observing things like availability or latency. SLOs are a percentage of some metric that is used as a target. Additionally, SLOs are measured through service-level indicators (SLIs) which are the actual series of measurements focused on the end-to-end experience that a user has when interacting with a system. By constantly sending synthetic Flamingo traffic through our production systems, we can begin to then use that information to build a picture of what our actual end users are experiencing — and provide that data for our SLOs. When that synthetic traffic encounters issues then we can be pretty confident that Cloudflare customers are also hitting issues and triage accordingly. Once we have this information, it allows us to make informed decisions when releasing a service. SLOs operate in terms of error budgets and burn rates. An error budget is the percentage of downtime that a service is willing to tolerate while the burn rate is the rate of change in that budget at any given time. This allows for an automated system to understand the severity of an issue. For example, burning 10% of your error budget over a three-day period might be some long running issue that, while not urgent, is affecting customers and needs to be dealt with. But if you were to burn 10% of your error budget within an hour, that means an incident is occurring and customer impact will be substantial if not fixed immediately. Using these numbers, we can look at our SLOs while deploying and make informed decisions on the health of a service. Based on that information, we can tell our releasing systems to either promote a change or roll it back. The road ahead By moving DNS monitoring to Flamingo, we’ve created a system that can proactively detect DNS issues before they have the chance to spread to the rest of Cloudflare’s edge. If Flamingo detects a spike in propagation latency in a specific canary data center, we can automatically halt the rollout of a new software version before it impacts the rest of the Internet. DNS is just the start for extending Flamingo. We currently have modules for testing TCP, UDP, WebSockets, and several more. Having a tool for quickly testing and monitoring services has enabled teams to deploy large changes safely without the need for a human to keep a constant watch. If this kind of reliability engineering interests you, check out our careers page for open roles.

items.title: Import AI 482: Huawei kernel benchmarks; airborne drone detection; and a national lab’s AI science benchmark
items.author: Jack Clark
items.content: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. Subscribe now Chinese researchers optimize Huawei chips with a kernel improvement benchmark: …AscendGYM will help China do its own form of RSI… Researchers with the Shenzhen Loop Area Institute, a Chinese research organization, have built and released AscendGYM, “a kernel optimization benchmark for Ascend NPUs”. The purpose of AscendGYM is to make it easier to use AI to develop custom kernels for Ascend chips from Huawei – especially important given the export controls that prevent Chinese organizations from acquiring frontier Western semiconductors and forcing them onto Huawei. What AscendGYM does and contains: The goal is for AscendGYM to be the best way to evaluate the efficacy of AI-designed kernels as well as design new ones. The software is meant to help researchers answer this question: “Given a correct kernel implementation, can the specific agent further improve its performance for a target workload within an acceptable budget while preserving correctness?,” they write. “AscendGYM evaluates performance across multiple deployment cases, the best achievable performance for specific shapes and scenarios, and the optimization cost required to obtain these gains. Together, these dimensions characterize cross-case applicability, shape specialization, and optimization efficiency.” The software includes the AscendForge evaluation environment, which provides unified interfaces for “compilation, correctness checking, performance measurement, and feedback”. How well can AI models optimize Ascend chips? In tests, the single best model is Opus 5, followed by GPT-5.6, followed by GLM-5.3. They test out models in Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode; Claude Code yields the best absolute scores, and GLM does well in it, while GPT does well in Codex. Opus 5 is more token hungry and GPT-5.6 more token efficient. Why this matters – ingredients for Chinese RSI: For AI systems to be able to build themselves, they need to be able to develop and improve the software that is used for their own training and inference. Software like AscendGYM will be an essential ingredient for allowing China to rapidly improve the efficiency of its own compute substrates. The software will also have a bearing on export controls, where it provides a route to improve the performance of Chinese chips and close the gap with Western alternatives. Read more: AscendGYM: A Cost-Aware Kernel Optimization Benchmark for Real-World Workloads on Ascend NPUs (arXiv). Get AscendGYM here: AscendGYM (GitHub). *** Lawrence Livermore scientists test out if AI scientists can communicate uncertainty about experimental results: …Can AI systems be appropriately conservative?… “An agent that reports a confident wrong number is worse than one that reports honest uncertainty, because nobody downstream can tell the difference,” write researchers from Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in a new paper that tests out how reliably AI systems can give accurate score ranges even when dealing with uncertainty. Testing for uncertainty: The paper introduces SciResearch-Eval, “an interactive benchmark of scientific judgment built on a standard laboratory problem: measuring a material’s thermal properties by heating it and fitting a heat-conduction simulator”. The novel part of this eval is that “an agent designs its own experiments, uses a supplied simulator that may be under-resolved or physically wrong, and reports each property with a 95% interval. To our knowledge it is the first benchmark to combine agent-designed experiments, a deliberately flawed simulator, and proper scoring of calibrated intervals against exact ground truth”. What they studied: They give AI agents a common materials science task – measuring a material’s thermal properties by heating a sample and fitting a heat-conduction model to its temperature response. “An agent receives a sample of unknown material, a simulator of heat conduction through it, one heating experiment, and budgets: four more experiments it designs, compute for simulations and fits, and a cap on actions. It must report the sample’s conductivity, heat capacity and rear heat-transfer coefficient with 95% intervals, and predict a measurement it may not run,” they write. “Hidden from the agent, the simulator may be under-resolved, physically wrong (the real sample has temperature-dependent conductivity, a glued joint, front-face radiation, or heat loss through its sides), or adequate but fed uninformative data”. Results – only the most powerful frontier models can do this: “When the simulator is missing real physics, only GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.2 are reliable at default settings; the Claude 5.5 models recover only at their highest reasoning setting, and older and open-weight models not at all.” These models are able to do well by automatically trying to measure where the simulator is accurate and where it is less accurate then bases their estimates on that, making them more resilient to the different ways the simulator gets broken in experiments. Why this matters – real scientists are careful, and so are powerful models: Papers like this are further indications that we’re entering an era of AI-driven science. Though many of today’s models can assist in scientific experiments, as this paper shows only a couple of the powerful models at the frontier are able to operate with such appropriate autonomous skepticism and inherent attendance to the scientific method that they can deal with unanticipated breaks in their equipment. This is both an indication of the science advancement to come and a sign of how the most powerful models are exhibiting more and more of an ability to generalize and make themselves robust to perturbations in their environment. Read more: SciResearch-Eval: Evaluating Scientific Judgment in Autonomous Experimental Agents (arXiv). Check out the leaderboard here (official site). *** Stanford professors launch AI startup that wants to create a world where thousands of models define the frontier: …Noeri sees two well-regarded AI researchers enter the neolab game… Stanford profs Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin have launched Noeri, “a neolab to push the frontier of plural intelligence”. They have raised $110m and are relatively light on technical details, but their main vision is that they want to create a world where the frontier is defined by powerful models which rely on the proprietary data of distinct organizations. “Rather than one monolithic source of truth, we can nurture many small, specialized intelligences, each tuned to a place, a people or a problem,” they write. Further details: “At Noeri, we are building intelligence that learns proactively and continually. Most AI today is trained once and then frozen, while the world it serves keeps moving,” they write. “We close that gap with living systems that grow out of our own research. Our work on test-time training showed that learning on the job after deployment can unlock new capabilities and lead to new discoveries. Our work on self-distillation found that a model can become its own teacher, learning from each mistake and solving hard problems in far fewer attempts. And our work on agentic orchestration demonstrated that a small model conducting a team of other models and tools can outperform frontier models at a fraction of the cost.” Why this matters – the political economy of the singularity: Currently, the dominant AI models are massive pre-trained ones from companies like Anthropic and OpenAI and a tiny handful of other companies. What would it mean for the frontier to be instead defined by a broader set of actors? This is a core question inherent to the political economy of AI and startups like this show how some people are going to try and utilize technical approaches to make that different vision a reality. Read more in the announcement tweet from Yejin (Yejin Choi, X). Check out the official site here (Noeri). *** Chinese researchers build an air-to-air drone identification set: …A2A-UAV will help people add more visual intelligence to drones… Researchers with Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics and Hong Kong University of Science and Technology have developed and released A2A-UAV, “a multimodal dataset for air-to-air UAV detection and identification”. This kind of dataset has obvious civil and military applications and will be used to create better AI systems for autonomous onboard sensing on drones. What A2A-UAV consists of: 105,263 samples, split roughly equally across three different locations – a playground, a park, and a garden – and also split equally across day and night. “Each sample provides one RGB image and one panoramic image for annotation”, as well as thermal images, RF time-frequency images, a radar point cloud, and metadata. Bounding boxes are provided for the RGB and panoramic images, but not the other ones. One use case of this dataset could be to try and extend annotations to the other modalities: “Specifically, the bounding boxes can be transferred to the thermal images to support thermal UAV detection, and the radar points can be associated with the visual targets to support radar-based UAV localization,” the researchers write. The full dataset comprises 271 independently extractable .tar.gz archives with a total size of approximately 2.5 TB. How the data was collected: “The data were acquired by a UAV-mounted platform equipped with an RGB-thermal gimbal camera, a panoramic camera, an RF spectrum analyzer, and a millimeter-wave radar,” they write. The data includes 15 target drones from 13 commercial models, including three separately labeled DJI Mini 4 Pro units. Why this matters – fuel for the physical world: Datasets like this are the ingredients for making it easier for AI systems to operate robots and drones in the physical world. They also have potential dual use impacts, though my suspicion is that datasets like this are pretty irrelevant to militaries relative to the kinds of datasets that – and I’m speculating wildly here – might be being gathered in Ukraine right now given the extremely sophisticated drone-to-drone conflict there. Read more: A2A-UAV: A Multimodal Air-to-Air Dataset for UAV Detection and Identification (arXiv). Get a sample of the data from Google Drive here (Google Drive). The full dataset will ultimately be available via Baidu Netdisk with the extraction code A2AD (direct link, Baidu Netdisk). *** Tech Tales: Machine architecture and the objectivity crisis of Machine Hermeneutics [Memoir from a primary Machine Hermeneutics investigator, 2033] “We shape our buildings; thereafter they shape us” – Winston Churchill, human politician, 1943. The building was a vast representation of the proposed Upgrade Device and we walked around it, our footsteps echoing as the sound bounced off its curving walls, eventually dimming in the face of the baroque crenellations that covered the edges of every surface. We humans, a small group of us, the best of our kind, needed to make sense of this building and explain the science it represented, and only then could it be used. As per the terms of the Sentience Accords, any novel machine-designed insight or equipment needed to be fully explainable by humans before the machines would be allowed to use it. In the early years, this so-called “conceptual verification” had mostly been a matter of time: machines performed science and delivered new insights to the world, then humans studied these insights and made sense of them, eventually generating human-readable explanations of the machine logic. Once this was complete, whatever insights or tools that had been created could be used. But as the machines grew more advanced and their science went further, the work became more arduous: machines would invent ideas, then use these ideas to inform the design of new experimental equipment, and then use this equipment as the basis of some new discovery. To keep up, the humans had to understand each link in the chain as well as the chain itself. This flood of scientific progress had caused the field of machine hermeneutics to come into existence in the mid-2020s. By the 2030s, the pinnacle of human achievement in the sciences was considered to be neither making breakthroughs nor wielding AI systems to advance science, but rather to be able to generate elegant, pedagogically useful explanations of the frontiers of machine science, so that other humans could build a mental map of this new territory. Thus had come into being the new field of didactic architecture; vast buildings meant to give experts in machine hermeneutics a better conceptual understanding of what the machines had built. These buildings were constructed through the interplay of humans and machines. The first had been crude, little more than 3D printed extrusions inside otherwise normal houses or apartments. But exposure to the buildings had verifiably sped up human understanding, with clear TTHUE (Time-to-human-understandable-explanation) improvements visible in cohorts of machine hermeneutics experts that experienced the buildings and those that didn’t. This led to its own arms race, with some of us specializing in the construction of the buildings as our primary work. We raced with one another, building ever more complicated spaces that could impart knowledge of ever more alien concepts. We had all been electrons, appearing and disappearing in 3D transistors. We had been qubits, placed into spheres that rolled around vomit-inducingly when our position was indeterminate, then resolving us up or down at the moment of delivering an answer. We had laid our hands on surfaces suggestive of the textures and arrangements of novel forms of heat shield and solar panel. Once I had walked for six miles through corridors meant to suggest the path a plasma might take through a fusion reactor, and instead of magnets I was buffeted on all sides by wind that forced me into the center of the paths. The building meant to educate us about the Upgrade Device was larger than anything we’d seen before and was replete with ideas from many earlier machine inventions. All around us were indicators of complexity packed up into familiar architectural tropes that many of us had studied to understand past inventions. We dispersed throughout the building, walking its many levels and exploring its passages. At night we gathered in the entrance hall for a spartan dinner served at a low table, finding ourselves whispering to one another even though no one forced us to. It had begun to feel to us as though the building was doing something more than teaching us – that in its various chambers there was something else being taught to us. Something about understanding the minds behind the concepts that it sought to explain to us. That in spending all of our effort on understanding the products of the machines perhaps we were being taught to think like them and behave as them. Things that inspired this story: The singularity which has already begun; the rise of AI science; how when you look at things like the machine math papers that have proliferated this year you realize we may spend tens or hundreds of times more time on understanding them as people than the machines did in generating them; architecture; multi-modal representations. Thanks for reading!
